english: Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.
usage: casual banmal, to a friend — the bare two-syllable 'got it' you breathe out
polite -요 version, keeps respect — use this with anyone you'd use 요 with (coworker, staff, stranger)
with 아 as a natural lead-in breath that softens it and marks the realization landing
past form, reacting to a past event they told you — also carries quiet sympathy ('oh, you went through that')
examples: 아, 그렇구나.
Oh, I see.
the bare reaction — just absorbing a new fact, no follow-up needed; 아 marks it clicking right now
A: 나 사실 부산 출신이야 / B: 아, 그렇구나. 어쩐지 사투리가.
A: I'm actually from Busan / B: Oh, I see. No wonder the accent.
A/B exchange: 그렇구나 receives the new fact, then pairs naturally with 어쩐지 when a clue suddenly clicks
A: 그 가게 월요일에 쉬어요 / B: 그렇군요. 알려주셔서 감사해요.
A: That shop is closed on Mondays / B: I see. Thanks for letting me know.
register lift: the polite 그렇군요 to a stranger who helped you — bare 그렇구나 here would sound too familiar
nuance: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. Literally it is 그렇다 'to be so' + the discovery ending -구나/-군요, which Korean reserves for something you have JUST taken in, so it always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization rather than neutral acknowledgment. The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. For a past event shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened,' which also lets you show quiet sympathy. The English-speaker pitfall is register: 'I see' feels neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is banmal; with anyone you keep -요 with it must be 그렇군요, and to a senior even 그러시군요. A second trap is using it as filler — overusing 그렇구나 to every line can read as only half-listening, so reserve it for genuine new info.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. It always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization, not neutral acknowledgment. Reacting to a past event, shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened,' which can also carry quiet sympathy.

Word by word it is 그렇다 'to be so' + the realization ending -구나, so it literally lands as 'ah, it IS so!' The real force is reactive discovery: 'oh, I didn't know that until just now.' It is not a statement of fact — it is the sound of new info settling in, which is why a flat present-tense statement can't replace it.

The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. Against 아 그래(요)?: that questions/checks the fact ('oh really?'), while 그렇구나 already accepts it and needs no answer.

Bare 그렇구나 is banmal — friends, juniors, kids only. With anyone you'd use 요 with (coworker, store staff, a stranger), use 그렇군요; to a clear senior or in deference, 그러시군요. The variant ladder is 그렇구나 → 그렇군요 → 그러시군요, each step adding respect; mismatching the step is the most common social slip.

'I see' feels register-neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar. A second trap: sprinkling 그렇구나 on every line reads as half-listening — reserve it for genuinely new info, and for a past event use 그랬구나, not present 그렇구나.

mistakes: Saying 그렇구나 to a boss, teacher, or elder — the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar; use 그렇군요 (polite) or 그러시군요 (honorific) instead.
Answering surprising NEW info with 그러게요 instead of 그렇군요 — 그러게(요) means 'right, same here' about a shared feeling, so it implies you already knew; for genuinely new facts use 그렇구나/그렇군요.
Using present 그렇구나 for something that already happened — if a friend tells you about a past event, the natural reaction is the past form 그랬구나, not 그렇구나.

english: True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.
usage: conceding a point after a beat of reconsidering — almost always opens the reply
agreeing once you reconsider — the most common full form, lands the concession
-네 marks realizing they have a point just now, the fresh 'oh' moment
casual, half-resigned agreement, slightly trailing off into a shrug
examples: 하긴, 그건 그래.
Fair enough, that part's true.
the bare concession — granting one specific point while you reconsider it on the spot
A: 지금 가도 차 막혀서 똑같아 / B: 하긴, 그냥 천천히 가자.
A: Even if we leave now traffic's the same / B: Fair enough, let's just go slow.
A/B exchange: conceding their logic and then changing the plan with a friend
A: 비 오는데 배달이 낫지 않아? / B: 하긴 그러네, 그냥 시키자.
A: It's raining, isn't delivery better? / B: Huh, you're right, let's just order.
the turn of mind: 하긴 그러네 marks the exact moment you switch your view to theirs
nuance: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It is the frozen, idiomatic shortening of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + the topic-contrast -기는), and as a reaction it almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. The contrast to keep clear is with 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair'; that reconsideration nuance is the whole point. It also differs from a flat 맞아 'you're right,' which is plain agreement with no 'hmm, on reflection' beat. Register-wise it is firmly banmal-flavored — everywhere among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock — but in formal or business speech it sounds too offhand; there you say 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not a strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant. Stronger/softer variants: 하긴 그래 (settled) vs 하긴 뭐 (half-resigned shrug).

structuredNuance.t: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. That 'I hadn't thought of it like that' reconsideration is the whole flavor.

Under the hood it is the frozen short form of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + contrast -기는), literally something like 'as for doing/it being so…'. But nobody hears the literal parts: as a reaction it just means 'true, fair enough, on second thought you're right.'

Against 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair.' Against flat 맞아: 맞아 is plain agreement with no reconsidering beat, while 하긴 specifically marks a fresh concession after a pause. Against 하긴 한데, which concedes BUT then objects — 하긴 alone simply yields the point.

Firmly banmal-flavored — natural among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock. In a formal meeting or to a superior it sounds too offhand; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. Softer/stronger variants: 하긴 그래 (settled), 하긴 뭐 (half-resigned shrug).

Treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant. Also don't expand it to 하기는 in speech as a reaction — the frozen 하긴 is what's natural.

mistakes: Treating 하긴 as full, firm agreement — it is a mild 'fair enough, you have a point,' not a strong yes; for committed agreement say 맞아 / 맞아요 or 그러게.
Using 하긴 in a formal meeting or with a superior — it sounds too offhand and casual; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요.
Spelling or saying it as the full 하기는 in conversation — as a reaction it is the frozen short form 하긴; 하기는 in speech sounds stiff and unnatural.

english: No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.
usage: reacting the moment an explanation lands and a small mystery resolves
with -더라 recalling the oddness you'd already noticed earlier
you'd already sensed something was up before the reveal — 했어 = 'I'd been thinking'
that's why it seemed that way
casual full-sentence reaction tying the reason to what you observed
examples: 어쩐지.
No wonder.
the bare one-word reaction when it all suddenly fits together — no answer expected
A: 나 어제 밤새웠어 / B: 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.
A: I pulled an all-nighter / B: No wonder you looked tired.
A/B exchange: 어쩐지 + -더라 ties the explanation to what you'd already observed
A: 그 사람 사실 사장님 아들이래 / B: 어쩐지. 다들 조심하더라.
A: He's actually the boss's son / B: No wonder. Everyone was careful around him.
the long puzzle clicks: a standing mystery finally gets its reason
nuance: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It is rooted in 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so under the hood it carries 'so THAT'S why,' and it loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed. The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': they share the 어쩌- stem and beginners blur them, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of the reason'). A softer near-synonym is 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why,' which is more explicit and complete; 어쩐지 keeps it punchy and can stand alone. It works in casual and softly polite speech alike — just surround it with 요-level verbs for politeness (어쩐지 …하더라고요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is a satisfied 'ah, no wonder.' A second trap: leaving the verb in plain present (어쩐지 피곤해) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' nuance — the natural shape adds -더라/-더라고요.

structuredNuance.t: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed.

Built from 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so literally it is 'somehow / for some reason.' In reaction use that flips to the satisfied 'so THAT'S why' — the reason that was missing has just been supplied, and you're confirming, not asking.

The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': same 어쩌- stem, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of it'). Softer twin 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why' is more explicit and complete; 어쩐지 stays punchy and can stand alone.

The word itself is register-neutral and works casual or polite — politeness comes from the verbs around it (어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라 to a friend, 어쩐지 …하더라고요 to someone you keep 요 with). On its own as a one-word 어쩐지, it's a light, everyday reaction fine with almost anyone.

Reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is 'ah, no wonder.' Second trap: a flat present (어쩐지 피곤해) loses the 'I'd noticed it before' feel — the natural shape adds -더라/-더라고요 to replay the earlier observation.

mistakes: Confusing 어쩐지 (no wonder, causal) with 어쨌든 (anyway, regardless) — they share the 어쩌- root but are opposites: 어쩐지 embraces the reason, 어쨌든 sets it aside.
Treating 어쩐지 as a question like 왜 ('why?') — it is a reaction meaning 'ah, that explains it,' so it expects no answer.
Forgetting the -더라 that usually follows — saying just 어쩐지 피곤해 (present) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' feel; the natural form is 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.

english: Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.
usage: dropping one thread for a new one you actually want to raise
leading warmly into the new topic — 말이야 softens the pivot
casual combo with 근데, doubling the 'shifting gears' feel
pivoting straight into a new question — a very common shape
examples: 그나저나 저녁 뭐 먹지?
Anyway, what should we eat for dinner?
the bare pivot to a fresh topic — drops whatever came before
A: 그래, 그것도 맞아 / B: 그나저나 너 이사 준비는 잘 돼 가?
A: Yeah, that's true too / B: By the way, is your moving prep going okay?
A/B exchange: closing one point, then raising what you actually care about
A: 그 얘긴 됐고 / B: 그나저나 주말에 시간 돼?
A: Enough about that / B: Anyway, are you free this weekend?
deliberate drop: abandoning a topic to set up a plan
nuance: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It comes from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way,' so it literally shrugs off the previous talk to pivot. The contrast you must keep sharp is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one — answer 'so what's the conclusion?' with 그나저나 and you've changed the subject instead of finishing. It also differs from 그건 그렇고 'that aside,' which is the slightly more composed, can-be-polite way to do the same pivot. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?). It is fine in everyday polite talk, but in formal writing or business email it is too chatty; there you use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라. English speakers map all of 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so they reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — that is the trap. A second trap: it is one word, 그나저나, not 그 나 저 나.

structuredNuance.t: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?).

It is worn down from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way / whichever way,' so literally it brushes 'this or that' aside. The real use is purely functional: it signals 'leaving all that — new topic now,' regardless of where the previous talk was heading.

The sharp contrast is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one. Closest twin is 그건 그렇고 'that aside,' which does the same pivot but is a touch more composed and can sit in polite/semi-formal talk.

Conversational and warm — fine in everyday polite talk and great between friends. In formal writing or a business email it is too chatty; there use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라 to change subject. Combine casually as 근데 그나저나 with friends for an even breezier pivot.

English maps 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so learners reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — but that's 아무튼/어쨌든. Also it is one word, 그나저나, and it is NOT 그러나 'however' (which contrasts ideas within one topic).

mistakes: Using 그나저나 to wrap up and conclude the current topic — that is 아무튼/어쨌든's job; 그나저나 switches to a brand-new topic, so it derails a conclusion.
Putting 그나저나 in formal writing or a business email — it is conversational and too chatty there; use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라.
Confusing it with 그러나 'however' because they look alike — 그러나 contrasts ideas within one topic, while 그나저나 leaves the topic entirely.

english: Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.
usage: wrapping up a tangent and driving to the point
closing a thought casually, letting the detail go
cutting past the explanation to land the warm message
examples: 아무튼 결론은 못 가.
Anyway, the point is I can't go.
the bare wrap-up to a conclusion — 결론은 underlines that you're landing the point
A: 설명하자면 길어 / B: 아, 그래? / A: 아무튼 도와줘서 진짜 고마워.
A: It's a long story / B: Oh yeah? / A: Anyway, thanks so much for the help.
A/B exchange: brushing past details to land the real message
A: 그래서 어떻게 됐는데? / B: 아무튼 잘 끝났어.
A: So how did it turn out? / B: Anyway, it ended fine.
glossing over the messy middle and giving the upshot
nuance: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It is built from 아무 'any' + the -튼/-든 'whichever' ending, so it literally says 'whatever the case, here's the point.' Two contrasts matter. First, against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one — they are not interchangeable even though both translate as 'anyway.' Second, against its closest twin 어쨌든: the two are near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.' It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.' The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'anyway' to cover both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners. A second pitfall: leaning on 아무튼 to cut off someone mid-explanation can sound impatient, so save it for genuinely 'enough detail, here's the upshot.'

structuredNuance.t: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.'

It is 아무 'any' + the -든/-튼 'whichever' ending, so literally 'whichever way it is.' The real job is to signal 'setting all that aside, the point is…' — it drives toward a conclusion, not away from the topic, which is what separates it from 그나저나.

Against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one. Against its closest twin 어쨌든: near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.'

Neutral and flexible — comfortable from casual chat (아무튼 그래) to polite speech, and acceptable in light writing. 아무튼 간에 bumps it toward a firmer 'regardless.' For very formal writing, 어쨌든 or 여하튼 can feel a touch more composed.

Using one English 'anyway' for both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners. Also, cutting someone off with 아무튼 mid-explanation can read as impatient, so reserve it for a genuine 'enough detail, here's the point.'

mistakes: Using 아무튼 to switch to a new topic — that is 그나저나; 아무튼 wraps up the current topic and drives to its point.
Assuming 아무튼 and 어쨌든 are always identical — they overlap heavily, but 어쨌든 leans more on 'regardless of the case,' often after weighing reasons, while 아무튼 is the plain 'anyhow, moving on.'
Stretching 아무튼 to mean 'either way both options are fine' — for genuinely weighing two outcomes, 어쨌든 fits better; 아무튼 just signals 'enough detail, here's the point.'

english: Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.
usage: setting the rest aside and proceeding to the outcome
stronger 'no matter what,' a firmer dismissal of the reason
interchangeable variant, handy for tone variety
leading to the outcome that stands regardless
examples: 어쨌든 됐어.
Either way, it's fine.
the bare 'regardless, that settles it' — closes off further debate
A: 그게 내 잘못은 아니잖아 / B: 이유야 어쨌든, 늦은 건 늦은 거야.
A: That's not my fault, though / B: Whatever the reason, late is late.
A/B exchange: acknowledging a reason but dismissing it as not changing the outcome
A: 환불은 어렵다고 하던데 / B: 어쨌든 한번 문의는 해 봐.
A: They said a refund is hard / B: Either way, try asking once.
pushing forward in spite of the obstacle
nuance: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so it literally carries 'however things turned out.' Its near-twin is 아무튼, and in most sentences they swap freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason' — it often follows a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든) — while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart, too, from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a new one rather than concluding it. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant. Two English-speaker traps: spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌 with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ); and overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection can sound dismissive, so use it when you genuinely mean 'that aside, let's proceed.'

structuredNuance.t: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant.

It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + past 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so literally 'however it turned out.' Functionally it concedes the point ('whatever the case may be') and pivots to the outcome that stands regardless — a concession plus a push forward.

Near-twin 아무튼 usually swaps freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason,' often after a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든), while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a NEW one rather than concluding it.

Neutral — fine casual or polite, and 어쨌든 간에 adds a firmer 'no matter what.' Slightly more composed than 아무튼 in writing, so it sits comfortably in semi-formal speech and reports; 어쨌거나 is a free variant for tone variety.

Spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌 with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ). And overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection sounds dismissive; reserve it for genuine 'that aside, let's proceed.'

mistakes: Spelling it 어쨋든 — the correct spelling is 어쨌든 (the middle syllable is 쨌, with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ); 어쨋든 is a very common but wrong typo.
Treating 어쨌든 and 그나저나 as the same 'anyway' — 어쨌든 concludes/sets aside the current point, while 그나저나 switches to a new topic entirely.
Overusing 어쨌든 to brush off every counterpoint — repeated, it sounds dismissive; reserve it for genuinely 'regardless, let's move on,' not for ignoring valid objections.

english: That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.
usage: partial agreement before a reservation — the cushion goes first
conceding casually with -지, lightest concession on the ladder
trailing off into hesitation, objection left soft and unstated
polite agreement before the but — for a senior or coworker
examples: 그렇긴 한데…
That's true, but…
the bare concede-then-hedge, trailing off so the objection stays gentle
A: 거기 싸고 좋잖아 / B: 그렇긴 한데 너무 멀어.
A: It's cheap and nice there / B: True, but it's too far.
A/B exchange: granting the point, then the real objection after -ㄴ데
A: 운동 좀 해야 돼 / B: 그렇긴 해요. 시간이 없어서요.
A: You should work out / B: That's true. It's just I have no time.
polite half-agreement softening a 'but' with a senior or coworker
nuance: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴 (그렇다 'be so' + the contrast-marking -긴), then -ㄴ데 swings the door open for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. The contrast to internalize is against a flat 아니 'no' or 그건 아니지 'that's not it': those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps the other person's dignity by agreeing partway first — Korean conversation strongly prefers this cushioned route. It also differs from plain 그런데/근데 'but,' which simply contrasts; the -긴 here adds a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that plain 그런데 lacks. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), it is never 그렇 긴; and skipping the concession and jumping straight to the objection, which in Korean lands as blunt and a little cold. Softer/stronger range: 그렇긴 하지 (light concede) → 그렇긴 한데 (full concede + clear but) → 그렇긴 한데 좀… (concede, then trail off to keep it soft).

structuredNuance.t: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴, then -ㄴ데 opens the door for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue.

Literally 'it IS so (그렇긴), but/and (한데)…'. The -긴 (from -기는) contrasts and concedes, so the real force is 'I'll give you that much, however…' — a built-in cushion, not a plain contrast. The listener hears the agreement first and the pushback as softened.

Against flat 아니 / 그건 아니지: those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps face by agreeing partway first — Korean strongly prefers this cushioned route. Against plain 그런데/근데 'but': 근데 just contrasts; the -긴 adds a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that 근데 lacks.

Plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal — to a senior or in polite talk use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요, then state the reservation. Softer/stronger ladder: 그렇긴 하지 (light) → 그렇긴 한데 (clear but) → 그렇긴 한데 좀… (concede then trail off).
Spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), never 그렇 긴 (and 한데 is its own chunk). And skipping the concession to jump straight to the objection — in Korean that lands as blunt and a little cold.

mistakes: Spacing it as 그렇 긴 한데 — 긴 attaches to the stem 그렇, so it is written 그렇긴 한데 (and 한데 is a separate chunk).
Dropping the concession and objecting head-on — Korean strongly prefers the cushion of 그렇긴 한데 before a 'but'; a flat 아니 or 그건 아니지 sounds blunt and cold.
Forgetting to make it polite when needed — to a senior, plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal; use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and then state your reservation.

english: Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.
usage: warm, emphatic polite yes — radiates welcome, not mere consent
casual version to a friend (NOT the connective 그럼 'then')
doubling up for extra warmth and reassurance
examples: 그럼요.
Of course.
the bare warm 'absolutely, yes' — full agreement, no hesitation
A: 자리 좀 맡아 주실 수 있어요? / B: 그럼요, 앉으세요.
A: Could you save my seat? / B: Of course, have a seat.
A/B exchange: agreeing warmly to a small request from a stranger or acquaintance
A: 이거 정말 가져가도 돼요? / B: 그럼요, 편하게 드세요.
A: Can I really take this? / B: Of course, help yourself.
reassuring a hesitant guest generously
nuance: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 plus the polite -요, so it literally affirms 'it certainly IS so.' Its near-synonym is 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously,' and the two often stack (그럼요, 당연하죠) for extra warmth; the subtle difference is that 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is a homograph clash: the SAME letters 그럼 also serve as the transition word 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자 'then let's go'). With the -요 attached, 그럼요 is almost always the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is the bare 그럼 plus a clause. Mixing them up makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…', which is confusing. A second pitfall: 그럼요 is emphatic and warm, so using it for a flat, lukewarm 'yes' overshoots — for a neutral factual yes use 네/예. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.

structuredNuance.t: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.
It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 + polite -요, so literally 'it IS so.' The real force is an emphatic, friendly 'of course! absolutely!' — affirmation with warmth, the opposite of a grudging yes.

Near-synonym 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously' often stacks with it (그럼요, 당연하죠); 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. Against a flat 네/예: those are neutral 'yes'; 그럼요 adds emphasis and warmth ('of course!').

그럼요 is the polite warm form — right for customers, seniors, strangers, hosting a guest. Plain 그럼 is the banmal version for friends. To a customer or elder, dropping to bare 그럼 for 'of course' sounds too casual; keep 그럼요.

Homograph clash: the same letters 그럼 also mean 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자). With -요, 그럼요 is the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is bare 그럼 + a clause. Mixing them makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…'. Also, 그럼요 is emphatic — for a flat factual yes use 네/예.

mistakes: Confusing 그럼요 (of course) with the transition 그럼 (then / in that case) — 그럼요 with -요 is an emphatic 'yes, of course,' while bare 그럼 + a clause means 'then…'; answering a question with the connective sense sounds off.
Saying plain 그럼 to a customer, senior, or stranger when you mean 'of course' — that is casual; the polite warm form is 그럼요.
Using 그럼요 to mean a neutral, lukewarm 'yes' — it is emphatic and warm ('absolutely!'); for a flat, factual yes use 네 / 예 instead.

english: Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'
usage: casual sympathetic agreement to a shared feeling
polite -요 version for someone you keep 요 with
stronger 'totally, I feel it' — ramps the agreement up
emphatic 'see, I told you' — pairs with 내 말이
examples: 그러게 말이야.
Right, exactly.
the bare strong 'totally, I feel the same' — full fellow-feeling
A: 날씨 진짜 춥다 / B: 그러게, 갑자기 겨울 됐어.
A: It's so cold / B: I know, it suddenly turned winter.
A/B exchange: warmly echoing a friend's complaint you already share
A: 진작 예약할걸 / B: 그러게, 자리가 없네.
A: We should've booked sooner / B: Right, there are no seats.
shared regret with a soft 'told you' undertone
nuance: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' It comes from 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending and works as a fellow-feeling echo. The contrast to fix is against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share ('yeah, I know, right?'), while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact you didn't know ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and you sound like cold weather is breaking news. A second near-synonym is 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying,' which is even more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이). Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up. The English-speaker pitfall is mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.' A second trap: because it can carry 'told you,' aiming it at a senior's mistake or complaint can sound smug, so keep it for shared feelings, not 'I-told-you-so' at someone above you.

structuredNuance.t: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up.

It is 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending — literally close to 'so it be / be that way.' The real force is fellow-feeling: 'right, I know, exactly — I felt the same.' It's an agreement noise, not a description, so don't parse it word-for-word.

Against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share, while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and cold weather sounds like breaking news. Near-synonym 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying' is more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이).

Plain 그러게 is banmal — friends and peers; with someone you keep 요 with use 그러게요. Because it can carry 'told you so,' it's best for shared feelings; aimed at a senior's complaint or mistake it can sound smug, so be careful upward.

Mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.' Second trap: its faint 'I-told-you-so' edge means it can read as smug if aimed at someone above you; reserve it for genuine shared feeling.

mistakes: Hearing 그러게 as the question 'why did you (do that)?' — it is an agreeing reaction meaning 'right, I know,' not an interrogative.
Using 그러게 to react to brand-new information — 그러게 echoes a feeling you ALREADY share; for news you just learned, use 그렇구나 / 그렇군요.
Saying plain 그러게 to a senior — it is banmal; with someone you keep -요 with, use 그러게요.

english: Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.
usage: reacting to their words or actions as YOUR reason — the cause is them
naming who prompted you — the trigger is the other person
with 하도 for 'so insistently,' adding 'they wouldn't stop'
justifying your reaction — '(you prompted me) so I did, obviously'
examples: 네가 그러길래 그랬지.
I did it because you said so.
the bare 'you prompted me, so I acted' — note the cause is YOU, not me
네가 먹고 싶다 그러길래 사 왔어.
You said you wanted some, so I bought it.
your action explained by their words — quotative 다 + 그러길래
A: 왜 먼저 갔어? / B: 다들 바쁘다 그러길래.
A: Why'd you leave first? / B: Everyone said they were busy, so…
A/B exchange: the reason trails off, the result left implied
nuance: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the connective -길래, and the defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself: that is exactly what separates it from plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that can take any subject. So 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained, neutral cause) is fine, but to say 'YOU kept saying it's good, so I tried it' you need 하도 맛있다고 그러길래 시켜 봤어 — the cause sits with them. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…). A close cousin is -기에, which means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form. The English-speaker pitfall: learners use 그러길래 for their own internal reason (because I was tired, because I wanted to) — for that you must use 그래서, since -길래 demands an external trigger from someone else. A second trap: when reporting speech, keep the quotative 다(고) — it is X-다고/-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…'); dropping the 다 garbles the 'because they said' sense.

structuredNuance.t: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. The defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…).

It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the reason connective -길래, so literally 'because (you/they) were doing/saying so.' Real use: 'since you said/did that, that's why I…' — your action framed as a direct response to their cue, with the spotlight on their prompt.

Against plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that takes any subject: 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained) is fine, but -길래 must point the cause at the OTHER party. Close cousin -기에 means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form.

Spoken and casual — natural in everyday talk, often trailing off (그러길래…). For an essay or report, the more literary -기에 is expected instead. It's neutral in politeness: you can attach polite endings to the result clause (사 왔어요).

Using 그러길래/-길래 for your OWN reason — it needs an external trigger from someone else; for 'because I was tired' use 그래서 (피곤해서), not 피곤하길래. Second: keep the quotative 다(고) when reporting speech — X-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…').

mistakes: Using 그러길래 (or -길래) for your OWN reason — it must react to someone else's words or actions; for your own internal reason ('because I was tired') use 그래서, e.g. 피곤해서, not 피곤하길래.
Writing -길래 in a formal essay or report — there the more literary -기에 is expected; -길래 is the casual spoken form.
Forgetting the quotative 다(고) when reporting speech — it is X-다고/-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…'); dropping it (X 그러길래 with no 다) garbles the 'because they said' meaning.

english: I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.
usage: soft polite inference from a clue you can see or hear
casual to a friend, same tentative hunch
negative version — 'seems like it's not the case'
hedging gently when unsure — stacks two softeners
examples: 그런가 봐요.
I guess so.
the bare soft guess from a hunch, no firm claim being made
불이 꺼져 있네요. 오늘 쉬는 날인가 봐요.
The lights are off. I guess they're closed today.
inferring from a visible clue — the evidence (불이 꺼져 있네요) comes first
A: 비 오려나 / B: 하늘 보니까 그런가 봐.
A: Is it going to rain / B: Looking at the sky, I guess so.
A/B exchange: 보니까 + 그런가 봐 grounds the guess in evidence
nuance: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright. The engine is the ending -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 'it looks like / I guess,' which marks a guess drawn from external evidence, so 그런가 봐요 = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' The contrast that matters is against -겠- and against 것 같다. -겠다 (그렇겠어요) is a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays more tentative; 그런 것 같아요 is very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the signs suggest so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.' Two English-speaker pitfalls: spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with 봐요 written separately as the auxiliary (not 그런가봐요); and don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd unless you mean it half-jokingly. Note the 봐 here is the verb 보다 in its inference sense, not 'look at it' — it is what makes this a hunch, not a command.

structuredNuance.t: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright, so it = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.'

Literally 'I look-and-see whether it is so' — the 봐(요) is 보다 in its inference sense, not the literal 'look at.' That's why the real meaning is a tentative, evidence-based 'I guess so,' not a statement and not a command to look.

Against -겠다 (그렇겠어요): a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays tentative. Against 그런 것 같아요: very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the outward signs suggest so.'

그런가 봐요 is the polite form; 그런가 봐 is casual to friends. Tone is gentle and non-committal, which makes it useful for not sounding too sure — good with seniors when you'd rather hedge than assert. Stack 그런가 봐요, 잘 모르겠어요 to hedge further.

Spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written separately (not 그런가봐요). And don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings/actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd; say 그런 것 같아요 or state it plainly.

mistakes: Spacing it as 그런가봐요 — the standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written as a separate word.
Using -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you infer about others/the world, not yourself; for your own state say 그런 것 같아요 or just state it, not 그런가 봐요.
Swapping it for confident -겠어요 when you only have a hunch — 그런가 봐요 is tentative (evidence-based guess); 그렇겠어요 sounds like a firmer 'it must be so.'

english: Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.
usage: reconsidering after listening — your view shifts on the spot
agreeing after a beat of reconsidering — 그렇네 marks the penny dropping
with -까 leading into a fuller clause that follows
after a second listen, re-judging with fresh ears
examples: 듣고 보니 그러네.
Now that you say it, yeah.
the bare 'on hearing it, you're right' — the mind changes on the spot
A: 이 색이 너한테 더 어울려 / B: 듣고 보니 네 말이 맞는 것 같아.
A: This color suits you better / B: Now that you mention it, I think you're right.
A/B exchange: coming around to their view after listening
듣고 보니까 그 식당 좀 비싸긴 했어.
Come to think of it, that restaurant was kind of pricey.
recalling and re-judging once the topic comes up
nuance: 듣고 보니 literally stacks 듣다 'to hear' + -고 보니 'having done and then found,' so it means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. The -고 보니 frame is a 'do X, then discover' construction (cf. 가 보니 'on going, I found,' 자고 보니 'after sleeping, I realized'), which is why it signals a fresh after-the-fact realization rather than a prior opinion. The contrast to keep is against 그러게: 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 듣고 보니 means 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it — and now I do,' so it foregrounds a CHANGE of mind. It also differs from 알고 보니 'as it turns out,' which reveals a hidden FACT rather than a shift in your opinion. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause. The English-speaker pitfall is reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not just chronology. A second trap: 보니 here is 'I found/realized,' not the purpose '-(으)려고 to hear,' so don't read it as 'in order to hear.'

structuredNuance.t: 듣고 보니 means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause.

It stacks 듣다 'hear' + -고 보니 'having done, then found' (cf. 가 보니 'on going I found'). So literally 'having heard, I find…'; the real force is 'on hearing it, I've reconsidered — and now I agree.' It marks a fresh realization, not a prior view.

Against 그러게 ('right, I already felt the same'): 듣고 보니 foregrounds a CHANGE of mind — 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it.' Against 알고 보니 'as it turns out': that reveals a hidden FACT, while 듣고 보니 reports a shift in YOUR opinion after listening.

Register-neutral — works casual (듣고 보니 그러네) or polite (듣고 보니 맞는 것 같아요), and it's a graceful way to concede to a senior because it credits their point. Use -까 (듣고 보니까) when a longer clause follows; 다시 듣고 보니 for a second listen.

Reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not mere chronology. Second: 보니 is 'I found/realized,' not purpose -(으)려고 'to hear,' so it does NOT mean 'in order to hear.'

mistakes: Reading 듣고 보니 as merely 'after listening' (time order) — in conversation it specifically signals 'now that you mention it, I've reconsidered and tend to agree.'
Using 듣고 보니 when you already held that view — it marks a CHANGE of mind prompted by what you just heard; if you already agreed, use 그러게 or 내 말이.
Confusing the -고 보니 'discover after doing' frame with -고 (으)려고 'intending to' — 듣고 보니 means 'on hearing, I found,' not 'in order to hear.'
